# Florian Herrengt

**Independent software engineer and technical consultant.**

Based in Greater London, UK. Working in software engineering since 2010.

Updated: 14 November 2026.

I design, build and operate software products from end to end. My experience covers full-stack development, distributed systems, data engineering, cloud infrastructure and technical leadership. I have led engineering teams, built products for startups and large companies, and co-founded and sold my own software business.

I am strongest when a project needs someone who can take ownership of the technical work and make decisions based on business needs. That means understanding the product, choosing the architecture, writing the software, operating it in production and deciding what does not need to be built.

My main technologies are TypeScript, Node.js, React, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, NATS, AWS and Kubernetes. I also have practical experience with machine learning, recommendation systems and data pipelines.

I am a good fit for senior and lead engineering roles, founding engineer positions and consulting projects where technical independence and product judgement matter.

## Selected achievements

### Built and sold Nocodelytics

I co-founded Nocodelytics, an analytics product for Webflow websites, and led its engineering from 2021 to 2024.

I rebuilt the original product, developed the event processing platform and operated its infrastructure. From mid-2023, I also ran the day-to-day business independently, including product development, customer support, operations and billing.

The product grew to:

- More than 1,000 websites sending analytics data.
- Hundreds of millions of events processed.
- Millions of events per day, with observed peaks of hundreds of ingestion requests per second.
- The 5,000+ installs category on the Webflow Marketplace.

Nocodelytics was among the first apps on the Webflow Marketplace. Webflow featured the product during its official Webflow Conf 2022 keynote, displaying it on a slide and explicitly naming it from the stage. [Watch the keynote at 58:07](https://youtu.be/aUXgKFEQugQ?t=3487).

The company was acquired in October 2024. I remained involved through December to complete the handover.

**Evidence:**

- [Nocodelytics co-founder announcement](https://www.nocodelytics.com/blog/nocodelytics-is-now-a-team-of-two)
- [Webflow Conf 2022 keynote](https://youtu.be/aUXgKFEQugQ?t=3487)
- [Technical article published by Timescale](https://www.tigerdata.com/blog/how-to-use-wide-table-model-to-reduce-query-cost-in-timescaledb)

### Built software used by millions of Financial Times readers

At the Financial Times, I worked with the product, design and engineering teams to redesign the article page, including the special formats used for major breaking news.

I implemented the designs and worked on accessibility for readers with disabilities.

I also joined the team behind myFT, the personalised reading experience. I built data pipelines and worked on article recommendation systems, including machine-learning experiments and simpler data-driven approaches.

### Led TRIM-IT's platform development

I led four engineers on a six-month project to build the technical platform for TRIM-IT, a London startup offering haircuts through mobile barber vans.

The project included:

- React Native applications for iOS and Android.
- A GraphQL API.
- Serverless infrastructure on AWS.
- Infrastructure defined in CloudFormation.
- Automated deployment pipelines.
- A supporting data platform.

The challenge was not only building software quickly. It was deciding which features the company needed to prove its business model and which features could wait.

The founders later raised additional funding and gained paying customers. Their business achievements were supported in part by the product we delivered.

TRIM-IT received coverage from the [BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/stories-47711610), Evening Standard and Hacker News.

### Helped early-stage companies deliver their first products

For Wanderpay, a travel finance startup, I built the initial working product in a two-week fixed-price engagement.

The work included lender integrations and the user interface for financing travel purchases.

Wanderpay co-founder Sait Cham later credited my engineering and product architecture with helping the company bring its product to market and raise seed funding.

I also worked at ContentCal, where I helped modernise an existing system, introduced GraphQL and improved deployment practices. ContentCal was subsequently acquired by Adobe.

These projects shaped how I work: understand the commercial objective first, then choose the simplest technical approach that can achieve it.

## Technical case studies

### 1. Nocodelytics: production event analytics

**Role:** Co-founder and lead engineer  
**Period:** 2021–2024  
**Technologies:** TypeScript, Fastify, NATS JetStream, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, TimescaleDB, GraphQL, React, Kubernetes, Helm, Longhorn

#### The problem

Nocodelytics needed to collect and analyse user activity across more than 1,000 Webflow websites.

It tracked events that conventional website analytics often did not handle well:

- Clicks on individual elements.
- Form submissions.
- Website searches.
- Webflow CMS collection and item interactions.
- Activity involving integrations such as Jetboost, Wized, Memberstack and Outseta.

Some customers had CMS collections containing more than 10,000 items.

The platform needed to identify which CMS item a visitor interacted with, even when Webflow did not provide a dedicated event hook. I implemented attribution by examining the rendered page and identifying the relevant collection and item.

The system also needed to handle sudden traffic spikes without slowing down customer websites or dashboard queries.

#### Architecture

The production architecture separated event ingestion, processing, storage and reporting.

**Event flow:**

1. **Client-side tracker:** A lightweight script automatically captured relevant interactions on each customer website.
2. **Ingestion API:** A Fastify service validated events, added server-generated identifiers and timestamps, and filtered unwanted traffic.
3. **Durable queue:** NATS JetStream stored accepted messages and separated ingestion from downstream processing.
4. **Enrichment workers:** Independent workers resolved site identities, parsed devices, processed location information, filtered bots and attributed CMS interactions.
5. **Analytics database:** ClickHouse stored event data for time-series analysis and dashboard queries.
6. **Application database:** PostgreSQL managed accounts, websites, dashboards, billing data and failed-event quarantine.
7. **Customer dashboard:** React and GraphQL provided the interface for creating and viewing analytics.

The main design principle was to keep ingestion independent of expensive processing.

If processing slowed down, the queue could absorb the backlog. Workers could then continue processing stored messages.

Workers acknowledged successful processing after the database confirmed the write. Events that could not be processed were sent to a quarantine store for later investigation and replay.

The queue and processing design supported retries and recovery. I did not rely on it as a guarantee against every possible form of data loss.

#### Database design

The analytics system initially used TimescaleDB, built on PostgreSQL.

One important decision was to use a wide table rather than a conventional normalised relational design for analytics data.

This reduced the work needed to assemble records during metric queries.

The result was documented in a technical article published on Timescale's engineering blog:

[How to reduce query cost with a wide table layout in TimescaleDB](https://www.tigerdata.com/blog/how-to-use-wide-table-model-to-reduce-query-cost-in-timescaledb)

The published comparison showed an approximately sixfold reduction in PostgreSQL's estimated query-plan cost for the example query. Actual query execution also became significantly faster, although the published figure is not a sixfold runtime benchmark.

The article includes schema examples, SQL queries, execution plans and an explanation of the design decision.

This experience also reinforced a lesson: database design should reflect how the application reads its data, not only how the data is logically related.

#### Moving from TimescaleDB to ClickHouse

As the product grew, I moved event analytics from TimescaleDB to ClickHouse.

I used a gradual migration rather than replacing the database in one operation.

The transition involved:

- Starting dual writes in September 2023.
- Sending new analytics events to both the existing PostgreSQL-based path and ClickHouse.
- Running the new storage path under production traffic before switching customer queries.
- Moving reads to ClickHouse after the new path had been tested.
- Removing the original event-write path last, in March 2024.

The migration took approximately six months and did not cause a complete production outage.

Because ingestion, processing and storage were separated, the change did not require rewriting the client-side tracker or public ingestion API.

#### Evaluating alternative architectures

I did not start with the final architecture.

I built and tested alternatives, including:

- A Go implementation of the ingestion API, benchmarked against the Node.js implementation.
- A fully serverless AWS processing pipeline using Lambda, Kinesis Firehose, S3, Glue and Athena.
- PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB storage designs.
- The later NATS and ClickHouse architecture.

The decision was based on performance, cost, deployment complexity and the operational requirements of a small business.

I selected the self-managed approach because it offered a better balance of cost and operational control for the product's actual workload.

I prefer to test technical alternatives rather than assume a newer language, service or architecture must be better.

### 2. Operating Nocodelytics: infrastructure and reliability

**Role:** Engineering and infrastructure owner  
**Technologies:** Kubernetes (k3s), Hetzner, Helm, Longhorn, Traefik, NATS, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, CI/CD

For much of Nocodelytics' life, I was responsible for the entire production system.

That included application development, infrastructure, databases, deployment, monitoring, security updates, backups and recovery.

From mid-2023, I managed these responsibilities without another full-time engineer.

#### Infrastructure

I migrated the production platform from AWS to a self-managed Kubernetes environment hosted on Hetzner.

The platform used k3s and Helm-managed services, including PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, NATS and supporting infrastructure.

Longhorn provided persistent-volume management.

The wider tooling included Traefik, Kubernetes deployment configuration, self-hosted source control, CI/CD pipelines and a private container registry.

I rebuilt the platform in December 2023 and completed the production migration during the following months, with traffic moved to the new environment in March 2024.

The change did not require a complete production outage.

The Kubernetes environment made service configuration and deployment consistent. Services could be managed through repeatable deployment procedures instead of manual changes to running machines.

#### Reliability

An analytics system has an unusual reliability requirement: if its public tracking endpoint is unavailable, some events may never be recorded.

I designed the system around several practices.

**Separate services**

The public ingestion API, processing workers and dashboard ran as separate deployments.

This reduced the risk that a slow analytics query or processing backlog would interfere with incoming events.

**Durable event processing**

NATS JetStream provided persistent message storage and controlled delivery to workers.

Failed events could be quarantined and investigated without blocking normal processing.

**Automated tests**

The project included 125 test files, covering application behaviour and supporting systems.

End-to-end tests sent real events through the staging ingestion endpoint and verified that the resulting data appeared in ClickHouse.

Database migrations were part of automated deployment pipelines.

**Monitoring beyond service uptime**

A service can be running while producing incorrect or incomplete data.

I added scheduled production checks to confirm that recent events were arriving and that enrichment fields were being populated.

The checks sent alerts when the expected data was missing.

I adjusted their time windows after observing false positives, so that alerts represented meaningful problems rather than normal fluctuations.

**Backups and recovery**

The system used several backup mechanisms, including storage snapshots, database dumps and off-site object storage.

I tested recovery procedures rather than relying only on successful backup jobs.

**Controlled deployments**

Deployment processes included immutable container images, versioned configurations, staged changes and rollback procedures.

I treated the ability to reverse a change as an important part of deployment quality.

#### Examples from production

The repository history contains specific examples of how I managed changes and problems.

- **September 2023:** I increased event-worker concurrency from 100 to 1,000 and adjusted retry behaviour to process a growing backlog.
- **September 2023:** I tested changes to the queue architecture and reverted unsuccessful approaches within minutes.
- **Webflow API migration:** A major API update required a rollback, additional fixes and a new release. The full correction cycle took approximately 72 hours.
- **ClickHouse migration:** I ran the old and new data paths in parallel for months before changing dashboard reads.
- **Infrastructure migration:** I prepared and tested the new Kubernetes environment before moving production traffic away from AWS.

Nocodelytics operated for approximately three and a half years without a customer-visible outage that took the product offline.

That result came from testing, monitoring, staged migrations and the ability to recover quickly. It was not the result of assuming that failures would never occur.

#### What this project demonstrates

Nocodelytics is the strongest example of my ability to own a complete technical product.

I built and maintained its application, data pipeline, infrastructure, integrations and operational processes.

I also handled customer problems, product priorities and commercial decisions.

The most important result was not the number of technologies used. It was that a small operation could deliver and maintain a commercial analytics platform while controlling cost and complexity.

### 3. Financial Times: recommendations and machine learning

**Role:** Full-stack engineer, contract  
**Period:** July 2017 – July 2018  
**Technologies:** Python, Keras, LSTM, K-means, AWS EC2, S3, data pipelines

At the Financial Times, I joined work on myFT, the personalised reading experience.

The objective was to recommend useful articles to paying readers.

This was not a straightforward optimisation problem. More article views did not necessarily mean a better experience for a subscriber.

#### The first approach

I experimented with deep-learning recommendation models using LSTM networks in Keras.

After approximately three months, the models gave only a small improvement over a simple baseline that recommended popular front-page articles.

The gain was too small to justify the additional complexity.

I consider spending that long on the complex approach before establishing stronger baselines a mistake.

#### What worked better

I moved to simpler methods using:

- Keyword matching.
- K-means clustering.
- Article metadata.
- Entity-based expansion of topics readers followed.

For example, a reader following Brexit could receive new articles about relevant political figures and developments, even when the article did not explicitly use the term Brexit.

User testing showed that readers were satisfied with the recommendations.

I also built data pipelines used by the data science team, including training workflows on GPU-enabled AWS EC2 instances and storage of model results in S3.

#### What I learned

A technically advanced solution is not automatically a better product.

A simpler method can be easier to test, explain, maintain and improve.

The 2019 RecSys paper *Are We Really Making Much Progress?* later examined a related problem: many neural recommendation approaches did not consistently outperform simpler baselines under careful evaluation.

This experience changed how I approach technical decisions.

I now establish a simple baseline before investing in complexity.

### 4. TRIM-IT: delivering a complete product under a deadline

**Role:** Project lead developer, contract  
**Period:** September 2018 – March 2019  
**Team:** Four engineers

TRIM-IT was an early-stage London company building an on-demand barber service using mobile vans.

The founders needed working software that could support the business and help demonstrate its potential to investors.

I recruited and led a team of four engineers.

We delivered the platform over approximately six months.

The system included React Native mobile applications, a GraphQL API, serverless AWS infrastructure and automated deployment.

Infrastructure was defined in CloudFormation so environments could be recreated consistently.

#### The difficult part was deciding what to build

At an early-stage company, engineering time is limited.

Every feature creates costs in development, maintenance, testing and support.

A large part of my work was helping the founders distinguish essential requirements from features that could wait.

The objective was to build a reliable product that could serve the company's immediate commercial goals.

That did not mean lowering code quality. It meant reducing unnecessary work.

This project helped me develop from someone focused primarily on technical delivery into an engineer who could also take responsibility for product decisions and business outcomes.

### 5. ContentCal: improving an existing product without rewriting everything

**Role:** Software engineer, contract  
**Period:** June 2020 – June 2021

ContentCal built tools for scheduling social media posts and analysing engagement.

I worked on a new product that had to integrate with an existing codebase.

Rather than replacing the old system, I added new capabilities and improved the architecture gradually.

My work included:

- Social media platform integrations.
- GraphQL APIs.
- Architecture improvements.
- Automated testing.
- CI/CD pipelines using GitHub Actions.

This allowed the team to make frequent deployments while continuing to support the existing product.

Colleagues later highlighted the simplicity of the solutions and the improvements to deployment and engineering practices.

ContentCal was acquired by Adobe, with the acquisition announced in December 2021.

[Adobe acquisition announcement](https://blog.adobe.com/en/publish/2021/12/08/adobe-to-acquire-content-cal)

## How I approach engineering

### Start with the problem, not the technology

I want to understand what the business needs to achieve before choosing tools or designing architecture.

I will use a new technology when it solves a real problem. I will also keep an existing system when replacing it provides little benefit.

My experience with machine learning, databases and infrastructure has repeatedly reinforced this approach.

### Make complexity earn its place

Every dependency, service and abstraction has a maintenance cost.

I prefer small systems with clear responsibilities and well-defined interfaces.

I am comfortable using distributed systems when the problem requires them. I do not believe that distributing everything automatically makes a system better.

### Design for change

Requirements change. Data volumes increase. External APIs change. Earlier technical decisions become unsuitable.

I try to make these changes possible without replacing entire systems.

Examples include the gradual ContentCal architecture changes, the Nocodelytics database migration and the move from AWS to Hetzner.

### Own production, not just development

My responsibility does not end when code is merged.

I care about whether it runs reliably, how it is deployed, how it fails, how problems are detected and how the team can restore service.

That is why I invest in testing, monitoring, migrations, backups and rollback procedures.

### Understand the cost of engineering

I have worked on products where my own income depended on what the software could deliver.

That changes how I evaluate technical choices.

A solution must be good enough to solve the problem reliably. It must also justify its cost.

Building less can be the right decision when the result meets the business need.

### Work independently, but communicate decisions

I have worked with founders, designers, product managers, engineers and data scientists.

I can take responsibility for architecture and implementation, but I also explain the trade-offs so that non-technical people can make informed decisions.

The best technical choice is not useful if it does not support the people and business that depend on it.

### Early work in machine learning: Skim.it

I was the first engineering hire at Skim.it, a startup working on document summarisation and natural-language processing.

I worked with researchers and data scientists to build software around resource-intensive machine-learning models.

My responsibilities included backend services, React interfaces, deployment and ML infrastructure.

I also helped lead two developers.

This was where I began using AWS Lambda and serverless architecture in 2015, while the technology was still new.

Skim.it later became associated with Deeper Insights, an AI consulting business.

### Data engineering: Lightful

At Lightful, I integrated large-scale Twitter data using AWS Kinesis.

I worked on analysis of audience overlap, posting behaviour and content recommendations.

This included implementing K-means clustering and applying methods from research papers to practical product problems.

## Since selling Nocodelytics

After the acquisition in October 2024 and the final handover in December, I took time to travel, explore new business opportunities and decide what I wanted to build next.

I continued to take occasional paid engineering and consulting engagements.

I have also explored several new software ideas and projects, including:

- **ModelNote** — [modelnote.io](https://modelnote.io)
- **Zuv** — [zuv.app](https://zuv.app)
- **RethinkLoop** — [rethinkloop.com](https://rethinkloop.com)

These are part of my exploration of new products and business models. I do not present them as established commercial successes.

Alongside this work, I have spent more time on technical writing, AI research, public speaking and developing a podcast.

My professional interests increasingly include how AI changes software engineering, how engineering teams should make decisions and which parts of development work remain valuable as implementation becomes easier to automate.

I continue to work as an independent engineer and consultant while exploring my next business.

## Background and independent projects

### Education

I have a master's degree in computer science from Ingésup in France.

I completed my education through a five-year work-study programme, known in France as *alternance*.

The programme combined academic study with paid work at software companies. The schedule alternated between time at university and time working for employers.

I began professional development work in 2010, before completing my degree.

This gave me practical experience with real customers, production systems and experienced engineers while I was still studying.

The programme was funded through employers and public education arrangements.

### How I started programming

I began using computers and writing simple programs when I was young.

As a teenager, I built games with RPG Maker and learned web development independently.

At 17, I spent approximately a year building a website for my secondary school in France. It included information pages and a map used during school open days.

I demonstrated that project when applying for my first development position.

That experience established a pattern I have followed throughout my career: learn what is necessary, build something useful and improve it through practical work.

### Organising PPE production during COVID-19

In 2020, when hospitals faced shortages of protective equipment, I helped organise a local 3D-printing operation to produce face shields for NHS workers.

I raised funding, established production at Craft Central and worked with medical staff to improve the designs.

The operation produced more than 1,000 face shields by early May 2020.

This was not a commercial software project. It was an example of taking an unfamiliar problem, organising resources and delivering a practical result.

- [Project write-up](https://blog.florianherrengt.com/3d-printing-ppe.html)
- [Fundraising page](https://www.gofundme.com/f/3d-printing-face-shields-for-nhs-workers)

### Building a self-driving RC car

In 2017, I built an experimental autonomous RC car using Arduino, Python, a camera, computer vision and machine learning.

The project was a way to learn by applying new concepts to a working physical system.

It was an early example of my interest in machine learning outside my professional work.

[Read the project article](https://blog.florianherrengt.com/self-driving-rc-car.html)

## Professional approach and commercial value

My experience combines three areas that are often treated separately.

**Engineering:** I can design systems, write software, investigate failures and operate applications in production.

**Product development:** I can work with founders and product teams to decide what to build, how to test an idea and what work should be avoided.

**Commercial ownership:** I have built software for clients, worked on fixed-price product contracts and operated a business where engineering choices affected my own costs and revenue.

This combination is especially useful in smaller teams, early-stage companies and projects with limited resources.

A client may need someone who can work across application code, infrastructure, databases and product decisions instead of requiring a separate specialist for every part.

That does not mean one engineer can replace a complete team in every situation. It means I can take responsibility for a wide part of the delivery process and identify where additional expertise is necessary.

I am particularly interested in projects where the engineering challenge has a clear business purpose and where I can help make both technical and product decisions.
